On October 15th, Elon Musk unveiled the new Tesla Roadster, and it broke the internet. The new Roadster flipped over a row of cars on SpaceX's thrusters, and it may have been more than a car demo. It may have been a preview of Tesla and SpaceX becoming one company.

Musk has written that idea off in the past, but more recently, he's said himself that his companies are "trending towards convergence." Since then, the speculation hasn't stopped. Barclays now expects SpaceX to buy Tesla, possibly within months. So what changed his mind? And what would they even look like put together?

The answer starts with the Roadster itself, because on paper, it's a Tesla, but it couldn't have gotten off the ground without SpaceX.

## An Engineering Flex

During the demo, the Roadster drove up a wall, hung upside down under a ramp, and then dropped off and rolled in midair. Later, it cleared a row of Teslas, a Semi among them.

And when you look at where they did it, it gets even more interesting. They didn't do this demo at a Tesla factory, but at a SpaceX rocket test site in McGregor, Texas, with SpaceX's thrusters bolted onto the Tesla. Before the first stunt, Musk told the crowd exactly what they were about to see.

<Quote collection="tesla-spacex" figure="clue_roadster_musk_collaboration_remark_oct2026" />

The Verge called it "completely useless as a viable product, but as a 30-minute flex of engineering muscle, it was truly a sight to behold."

And that was exactly the point. It was a joint demonstration, an opportunity for Elon to flex Tesla and SpaceX's engineering prowess and provide a taste of what the two companies could build together.

But Elon didn't always think the companies were a fit.

## Musk Changed His Tune

Back in 2016, Musk said there was no "strong product rationale to combine SpaceX and Tesla." But last year, he posted that "my companies are, surprisingly in some ways, trending towards convergence." He's even begun shutting down the question on analyst calls, stating that "we can't talk about combining companies and that kind of thing on an earnings call. It has to be done with the appropriate processes."

The press has been circling the topic all year. Bloomberg and CNBC both reported Musk had weighed folding the two together. JPMorgan called it "strategically coherent on paper." Even SpaceX's president said a merger "might make Elon's life a little easier."

And people are betting real money on it. By the morning after the Roadster, the odds of a deal by March had jumped from 29% to 56%, cooling down to 45% about a day later.

<DashboardEmbed collection="tesla-spacex" slug="the-tune-changes" />

Nonetheless, the companies continue to become more intertwined. Tesla invested $2 billion into xAI. SpaceX buys Tesla's Megapack batteries for its AI data centers. Grok is in Tesla's cars. And the two companies have also said they plan to build a chip factory together.

And the strongest signal for a merger is SpaceX's behavior itself. This year alone, it bought xAI, and with it Grok and X. It went public at a valuation of about $1.8 trillion, and it's already spent $60 billion in stock this year to buy Cursor. So if you're curious how Elon might structure the deal, there's a lot of precedent to work off of. And Tesla is the last big piece.

<DashboardEmbed collection="tesla-spacex" slug="the-last-big-piece" />

## The Deal on the Table

So what if they combined? What if Tesla's factories and SpaceX's technology were one company?

Barclays thinks it might look like this. In a note on October 14th, its analyst wrote that he expects SpaceX to buy Tesla in a stock-for-stock deal, which means Tesla shareholders would get SpaceX shares instead of cash. SpaceX is now the more valuable of the two. At the close of October 16th, it was worth about $1.98 trillion, compared with about $1.4 trillion for Tesla. So each Tesla share was worth about 2.43 SpaceX shares, before the premium Barclays expects Tesla holders to get. Together, that's a company worth about $3.4 trillion.

<DashboardEmbed collection="tesla-spacex" slug="the-deal-on-the-table" />

And one man would have voting control of the whole thing.

But this wouldn't be just an exercise in financial engineering. There are significant synergies between the Tesla and SpaceX businesses that, if you bundle them together, make it a much stronger asset.

## Where It Clicks

Today Tesla is still primarily a car company. It brought in about $95 billion of revenue last year, and about three quarters of that came from its car business. What it's best at is building complicated hardware at enormous scale. Last quarter alone, it delivered more than 486,000 cars. But it also has a fast-growing energy business, selling the giant Megapack batteries that back up power grids, and increasingly, AI data centers.

But investors aren't paying $1.4 trillion for the cars. Tesla's value is a bet on autonomy, in two parts. The first is self-driving. About 1.5 million people already pay for Tesla's self-driving software, and Tesla now runs robotaxis with nobody behind the wheel in six cities. It's still small, with only a few million dollars of fares so far by our estimate, but Tesla has built a line in Texas to make more than 125,000 Cybercabs a year, a car designed from the start to be a robotaxi. The second bet is Optimus, Tesla's humanoid robot. They aren't on sale yet, and the newest version hasn't been shown, but Tesla is planning for a million robots a year. And Musk has said about 80% of Tesla's value will be Optimus.

<DashboardEmbed collection="tesla-spacex" slug="the-autonomy-bet" />

SpaceX is a more layered business. Shaun Maguire, the Sequoia partner who runs its investments in SpaceX, told Bloomberg he thinks of it in five layers.

Layer one is launch, the foundation. SpaceX flew 170 missions last year, and it says it carried more than 80% of everything the world sent to orbit. If you need to put something big into space, there's essentially one call to make. And Starship, its rocket built to be fully reusable and carry 100 tons at a time, put its first satellites into orbit last month.

Layer two is connectivity. Starlink now has 9,600 satellites and 12 million subscribers, double what it had a year ago, with margins around 60% before it spends on growth. So this is a proven layer, and the cash engine for the whole company.

Layer three is compute. SpaceX is now a hyperscaler, which basically means a company that rents out computing power the way Amazon and Microsoft do. It has about 1.4 gigawatts of AI computing. Google rents capacity from it, and Anthropic alone has agreed to pay a massive $1.25 billion a month. It's almost all on the ground today, but SpaceX wants to put data centers into orbit, with its first AI satellites planned for 2027.

Layer four is the models and the apps that run on them: Grok, X, and now Cursor. And in Maguire's words, "most investors don't know how to assess where SpaceX, SpaceX AI really is today," meaning investors are underestimating the potential value of it.

The fifth layer is all the other bets. Think Terafab, the chip factory it's planning with Tesla, and someday a moon base.

And the money is moving up the layers fast. Last year, Starlink was about 60% of SpaceX's revenue, launch about a fifth, and AI less than that. By the second quarter, AI was already a third of SpaceX's $7.8 billion in revenue, and launch was down to about an eighth.

<DashboardEmbed collection="tesla-spacex" slug="the-five-layers" />

And this is where things get really interesting. Step back, and look at what each one has. SpaceX has launch, satellites, data centers and AI. Tesla has power, manufacturing at scale, robotics and autonomy. And all of these are very accretive and make each other better.

You can already see it. Tesla's batteries are helping power SpaceX's AI, and SpaceX's Starlink is going into the Cybercab. Grok is already in Tesla cars, and Musk wants it in all of the Optimus humanoid robots.

<DashboardEmbed collection="tesla-spacex" slug="the-loop" />

Essentially, if they consolidate into one company, the synergy is indisputable, and the scale of the business makes life a lot easier too.

## One Balance Sheet

So let's look at the numbers, starting with each company on its own. Tesla brought in about $95 billion of revenue last year. That's still enormous, but the profits have gotten thin. In the second quarter, its operating income was under $400 million, and most of what it earned on paper came from the rising value of its SpaceX shares.

SpaceX is smaller, but growing much faster. It made about $19 billion last year and $7.8 billion in the second quarter alone, up 92% from a year earlier. SpaceX is still losing money because it's pouring cash into the build-out, about $18 billion of capex in a single quarter, most of it on AI. However, it's also still sitting on $100 billion in cash, mostly from the recent IPO.

<DashboardEmbed collection="tesla-spacex" slug="each-on-its-own" />

Put them together, and you get a company that brought in about $114 billion of revenue last year, holds about $144 billion of cash, and is worth roughly $3.4 trillion, which would make it one of the most valuable companies on the planet.

<DashboardEmbed collection="tesla-spacex" slug="one-balance-sheet" />

And yes, that is an extremely premium price. $3.4 trillion is about 30 times what the two made in revenue last year, and SpaceX alone is valued at about a hundred times its revenue. Investors aren't paying for today's business, they're paying for the most comprehensive set of bets on the market. These two are already at the front of some of the biggest markets there are, from autonomous driving to space, AI and computing. And they're positioned for the frontier ones that barely exist yet, like data centers in orbit or humanoid robots.

Musk, however, thinks the opportunity is a lot bigger. On SpaceX's first earnings call, he said that the company's "internal projections for reaching a trillion dollars in revenue" had "moved up from 2031 to 2030." Last year, he wrote that 80% of Tesla's value will be Optimus. And on October 14th, the night before the Roadster event, replying to a post about investor Ron Baron's forecast of $20 to $50 trillion, he wrote, "Unless there is a major world war, SpaceX probably gets to" more than $100 trillion in less than 10 years.

Now, I'm not underwriting that $100 trillion number, or giving a view on whether they'll get there. But getting from $2 trillion today to $100 trillion in ten years would take serious growth: SpaceX's stock would have to compound at roughly 48% a year, every year, for a decade.

<DashboardEmbed collection="tesla-spacex" slug="a-hundred-trillion" />

So the price is a bet on Musk being right about the future, and if the two combine, he'd have almost unilateral control of how they get there.

## Where It Lands

But a deal this big comes with strings, and the first one is control. Musk owns about a fifth of Tesla, and at SpaceX, he controls more than 80% of the votes, through special Class B shares that carry ten votes each. So if Tesla's stock were swapped into SpaceX's, Musk would end up with voting control of the whole combined company. Barclays puts it at more than half the votes. And Musk has been clear that this matters to him: "I don't feel comfortable wielding that robot army if I don't have at least a strong influence."

<DashboardEmbed collection="tesla-spacex" slug="control" />

So when could this happen? Both companies report earnings this week: SpaceX reported on October 20th, and Tesla reports on the 21st. But don't expect a deal on an earnings call. Musk has said himself that this has to go through "the appropriate process," and the betting markets give it about a 4% chance before November. The date to watch is Tesla's annual shareholder meeting, due by December 6th. Barclays sees that as one possible moment. If they announce a deal before the meeting, Tesla's shareholders could vote on it right there.

Whether or not it happens at that meeting, it's clear that Musk sees his businesses converging. That's a big change from ten years ago, when he said there was no strong reason to put SpaceX and Tesla together. Now he's openly discussing it, and with the Roadster demo, he spent a night showing us just what that might look like. The only question left is whether he makes it official.
